title: ERC-1271: Standard Signature Validation Method for Contracts (Final)
quote: // bytes4(keccak256("isValidSignature(bytes32,bytes)") bytes4 constant internal MAGICVALUE = 0x1626ba7e; ... MUST return the bytes4 magic value 0x1626ba7e when function passes. MUST NOT modify state (using STATICCALL for solc < 0.5, view modifier for solc > 0.5). MUST allow external calls ... `isValidSignature()` should not be able to modify states in order to prevent `GasToken` minting or similar attack vectors. ... The specific return value is expected to be returned instead of a boolean in order to have stricter and simpler verification of a signature. ... Since there are no gas-limit expected for calling the isValidSignature() function, it is possible that some implementation will consume a large amount of gas. It is therefore important to not hardcode an amount of gas sent when calling this method on an external contract ... Note also that each contract implementing this method is responsible to ensure that the signature passed is indeed valid, otherwise catastrophic outcomes are to be expected.

title: ERC-7739: Readable Typed Signatures for Smart Accounts (Draft)
quote: /// @dev This implementation is NOT safe. function isValidSignature(bytes32 hash, bytes calldata signature) external override view returns (bytes4) { ... address signer = ecrecover(hash, v, r, s); ... if (signer == owner) { return 0x1626ba7e; } else { return 0xffffffff; } } ... When multiple smart accounts are owned by a single EOA, the same signature can be replayed across the smart accounts if the `hash` does not include the smart account address. Unfortunately, this is the case for many popular applications (e.g. Permit2). As such, many smart account implementations perform some form of defensive rehashing. First, the smart account computes a final hash from minimally: (1) the hash, (2) its own address, (3) the chain ID. ... Defensive rehashing can be implemented with EIP-712, but a straightforward implementation will make the signed contents opaque.

title: ERC-6492: Signature Validation for Predeploy Contracts (Final)
quote: However, if the contract is not deployed yet, ERC-1271 verification is impossible, as you can't call the `isValidSignature` function on said contract. ... The signature verifier MUST perform a contract deployment before attempting to call `isValidSignature` if the wrapper signature format is detected. The wrapper format is detected by checking if the signature ends in `magicBytes`, which MUST be defined as `0x6492649264926492649264926492649264926492649264926492649264926492`. ... concat(abi.encode((create2Factory, factoryCalldata, originalERC1271Signature), (address, bytes, bytes)), magicBytes)

title: OpenZeppelin Contracts v5.7.0 — SignatureChecker
quote: Checks if a signature is valid for a given signer and data hash. If the signer has code, the signature is validated against it using ERC-1271, otherwise it's validated using `ECDSA.recover`. NOTE: Unlike ECDSA signatures, contract signatures are revocable, and the outcome of this function can thus change through time. It could return true at block N and false at block N+1 (or the opposite). ... if (signer.code.length == 0) { (address recovered, ECDSA.RecoverError err, ) = ECDSA.tryRecover(hash, signature); return err == ECDSA.RecoverError.NoError && recovered == signer; } else { return isValidERC1271SignatureNow(signer, hash, signature); }

title: OpenZeppelin issue #6773 — Revisit SignatureChecker ECDSA/ERC-1271 ordering once EIP-8151 + EIP-8298 ship
quote: Opened 2026-09-15 by Amxx, labelled "on hold". #4951 changed the order of operations in SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow ... to an explicit dispatch on whether the signer has code. The reason is that with the "ECDSA check, fallback to ERC-1271 if invalid" form, an account whose address is derived from an ECDSA key can never fully revoke that key at the application level: whatever its isValidSignature returns, a raw ECDSA signature from the original key keeps validating. Dispatching on code.length lets such an account migrate away from the key entirely, at the cost of one EXTCODESIZE and of making ERC-1271 the only accepted scheme once the account has code.

title: Alchemy — ERC-1271 Signature Replay Vulnerability (disclosure)
quote: On October 27th 2023, Alchemy discovered a ERC1271 contract signature replay vulnerability that affected a large number of smart contract accounts (SCA), and led to risks when interacting with several applications. ... affected: LightAccount, Kernel (Zerodev), Biconomy, Soul Wallet, EIP4337Fallback (Gnosis Safe integration), AmbireAccount, SmartAccount (OKX), BaseWallet (Argent), Fuse Wallet; applications: Permit2 and Cowswap. Gnosis Safe was not vulnerable to this attack vector. ... curiousapple, an independent security researcher, had found the same vulnerability a month prior. ... At this point, no funds are at risk and the impact to applications is fairly limited.

quote: Opened 2020-07-08 by frozeman, merged 2020-07-09. Body: "This changes the proposal to use a `bytes32` hash for the signature to prevent the requirement of specific implementation checks within this signature verification functions. Those can be either done off-chain, or in other smart contract functions, and funnel those to this function to verify the signature." The automerge bot declined: "Hi! I'm a bot, and I wanted to automerge your PR, but couldn't because of the following issue(s): - EIP 1271 requires approval from one of (@izqui, @phabc, @abandeali1, @catageek, @shrugs, @frangio)". 3esmit objected: "I think this change is bad. I have use-case where I need to pass the whole data to the contract, not just it hash, because the data defines if the signature can be validated or not." pedrouid replied: "we should aim ERC-1271 to provide the same level of functionality as ecrecover does off-chain... introducing additional validation seems to be out-of-scope of this standard IMO". frozeman concluded: "Any extra validation scheme should be standardised separately."
